questions.stem: What does the proverb 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE' mean?

options.option_text: Sewing is a time-consuming activity
Addressing a problem early prevents it from becoming bigger
Nine is the ideal number of stitches in needlework
Saving time is more important than saving money

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A stitch in time saves nine' = if you repair a small problem promptly, you prevent it from becoming a much bigger problem requiring nine times more effort later. Origin: stitching a small tear early prevents needing to stitch a much larger tear. Example: 'He fixed the leaking pipe before monsoon — a stitch in time saves nine.' Trap: A and C are literal, non-idiomatic interpretations.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates the proverb 'BARKING DOGS SELDOM BITE'?

options.option_text: A dog that growls eventually attacks its owner
A person who makes loud threats rarely follows through with action
Silence is more threatening than noise
People who talk a lot have more friends

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Barking dogs seldom bite' = people who make loud threats or complaints are usually not dangerous and rarely follow through with their threats. Example: 'Don't worry about his angry emails — barking dogs seldom bite.' Trap: A is the literal (and incorrect) interpretation; C presents a different idea; D is unrelated.

questions.stem: What does the proverb 'BIRDS OF A FEATHER FLOCK TOGETHER' mean?

options.option_text: Wild birds form large groups during migration
People with similar tastes and interests tend to form groups
Common interests lead to rivalry
Groups are stronger than individuals

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Birds of a feather flock together' = people who are similar in character, interests, or background tend to associate with each other. Example: 'All the chess club members are introverts — birds of a feather flock together.' Trap: A is the literal (ornithological) reading; C (rivalry) is the opposite of the proverb's meaning; D (strength in numbers) is a different proverb ('United we stand...').

questions.stem: What does 'DON'T PUT ALL YOUR EGGS IN ONE BASKET' advise?

options.option_text: Handle fragile items with care
Diversify your risks rather than depending on one option
Plan ahead for future difficulties
Avoid taking risks altogether

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Don't put all your eggs in one basket' = don't risk everything on a single venture; spread your risk across multiple options. Origin: if you carry all eggs in one basket and drop it, you lose all eggs. Example: 'He invested in stocks, gold, and real estate — he didn't put all his eggs in one basket.' Trap: C ('plan ahead') describes a different proverb; D ('avoid risks') is the opposite — the proverb allows risks but advises diversification.

questions.stem: Which proverb best fits this situation: 'Ravi spent all his savings and now struggles to buy food, while his neighbour Suresh saved every month and is financially secure.'

options.option_text: Make hay while the sun shines
Every cloud has a silver lining
A penny saved is a penny earned
Look before you leap

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'A penny saved is a penny earned' = money saved is as valuable as money earned; thrift is as important as earning. The situation directly contrasts a spendthrift (Ravi) and a saver (Suresh), perfectly illustrating this proverb. Trap: 'Make hay while the sun shines' = take advantage of opportunities when they arise (about timing, not savings); 'Every cloud has a silver lining' = every difficulty has some positive aspect (about optimism); 'Look before you leap' = think before you act (about caution in decisions).

questions.stem: What does the proverb 'THE GRASS IS ALWAYS GREENER ON THE OTHER SIDE' mean?

options.option_text: Nature thrives better on the other side of a fence
Other people's situations always seem better than one's own
Distant goals are always more attractive than near ones
You should always travel to explore new places

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The grass is always greener on the other side (of the fence)' = other people's circumstances, achievements, or possessions always seem more appealing than our own, even when they may not actually be better. Example: 'He thinks his colleague's job is more interesting — the grass is always greener.' Trap: A is the literal horticultural interpretation; C is close but 'grass is greener' refers to other people's lives/things, not distant goals specifically.

questions.stem: What does 'ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS' mean?

options.option_text: Loud noises are more effective than quiet ones
What people do reveals more about them than what they say
Speaking confidently is the key to success
Silent people are untrustworthy

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Actions speak louder than words' = people's actual behaviour is more telling than their promises or claims. Example: 'He promised to help but never showed up — actions speak louder than words.' Trap: A is a literal, non-idiomatic reading; C elevates speech over action (the opposite of the proverb's lesson); D draws a wrong conclusion about silent people.

questions.stem: What does the proverb 'EVERY CLOUD HAS A SILVER LINING' convey?

options.option_text: Clouds reflect sunlight from their edges
Even the worst situations have some positive aspect
Good times always follow bad times in a cycle
One should look for hidden treasures in unexpected places

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Every cloud has a silver lining' = in every difficult or negative situation, there is something positive to be found. Example: 'He lost his job but found a better one — every cloud has a silver lining.' Trap: A is the literal meteorological reading; C (cycles of good and bad) is a subtly different idea — the proverb is about finding positives IN bad situations, not about them being succeeded by good times; D (hidden treasures) extends the metaphor too far.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates 'HASTE MAKES WASTE'?

options.option_text: A factory recycling its waste products efficiently
A surgeon who rushed the operation made errors that required corrective surgery
A cook who worked quickly finished before the others
A student who studied slowly failed the exam

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Haste makes waste' = acting too quickly often leads to mistakes that require more effort to correct — doing things in a rush wastes time and resources. The surgeon example shows: rushing → errors → corrective surgery (more effort than if done carefully the first time). Trap: C shows a cook who was FAST and SUCCESSFUL (disproves haste makes waste); D shows a slow student who failed (relates to insufficient effort, not excessive haste).

questions.stem: What does 'WHEN IN ROME, DO AS THE ROMANS DO' advise?

options.option_text: Travel to Rome to learn Roman customs
Follow the local customs and practices wherever you are
Adopt an aggressive attitude when dealing with unfamiliar people
Obey the rules of your home country even abroad

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'When in Rome, do as the Romans do' = when you are in an unfamiliar place or situation, you should follow the local customs, traditions, or practices of the people there. Example: 'At the Japanese dinner, she removed her shoes and sat on the floor — when in Rome!' Trap: A is an overly literal travel suggestion; D is the opposite (your home rules abroad); C is unrelated to the proverb's message.
